item.title: Better Models Aren’t Enough: China’s AI Race Turns to Cost, Products and Paying Users
item.dc:creator: TechNode Staff
item.description: Editor’s note: This article was written by Lucia, a TechNode reporter. item.content:encoded:
Editor’s note: This article was written by Lucia, a TechNode reporter.

At a Sept. 1 online media briefing for the 23rd UBS Securities A-Share Seminar, discussion around China’s AI sector centered on a practical question: can lower costs and wider AI use translate into real business value?

UBS Securities China internet analyst Xiong Wei highlighted three themes to watch in China’s large-model sector: model capability, “token ROI” and monetization. While Chinese developers continue to improve their models — particularly in coding and agentic capabilities — companies using AI are becoming more selective about how much intelligence they actually need for a given task.

That marks a shift from “token-maxxing,” or encouraging more AI usage, toward “token optimization,” Xiong said. After rising AI bills made it harder for enterprises to measure the economic value generated by their token consumption, buyers have begun paying greater attention to the balance between performance and price. Xiong said that trend favors Chinese open-source models, whose improving capabilities and lower costs make them increasingly viable for repetitive or lower-risk workloads.

Xiong estimated that some leading Chinese models may cost less than one-tenth as much to develop as overseas peers, while average API pricing can be around 10% to 20% of international competitors. However, cheaper AI does not automatically translate into more revenue.

Kenneth Fong, UBS’s head of China internet research, said China’s major internet platforms face a more fundamental constraint: user traffic and time spent on mobile devices are no longer growing much. AI can lower content-production costs and make advertising or recommendation systems more effective, but consumers still have limited time and attention. He used AI-generated short dramas as an example: producing more shows at lower cost does not mean they will capture more of viewers’ time and attention.

A new experiment from Mango TV illustrates both sides of that equation. The Later Journey to the West, an AIGC-produced fantasy series, debuted on Mango TV and in Hunan Satellite TV’s prime-time slot on Aug. 31, becoming China’s first AIGC long-form series to reach a satellite-TV prime-time slot.

Adapted from an anonymously written late-Ming or early-Qing fantasy novel of the same name, the story follows a new generation of characters who reunite for another journey to obtain Buddhist scriptures after the originals are misunderstood.

Its first season is planned to run for 30 episodes of about 40 minutes each. The series is being made with Mango Lingchuang, Mango TV’s in-house AIGC production platform, which had served more than 40,000 professional users and supported over 3,900 projects by mid-2026.

The platform generated 109 character assets and 143 scene assets for the series, while the project is also testing a “produce, review and broadcast in parallel” model, allowing later episodes to remain in production as earlier ones air. The series also showed some early audience traction: real-time ratings for its Aug. 31 premiere ranked first among provincial satellite channels in the same time slot, according to ITHome, while ChinaTimes reported that it had logged 27.57 million plays on Mango TV by Sept. 2.

Yet whether those efficiencies and early audience gains can translate into a sustainable business remains unclear. Before the series aired, Hunan’s broadcasting regulator asked the project team to explore both a workable technical path for AI-powered long-form storytelling and a commercialization path for AIGC seasonal dramas.

That challenge echoes points made by both Xiong and Fong: as AI becomes cheaper to use and lowers production costs, the focus is shifting from how much AI can produce to whether its use can generate sufficient economic value.

item.title: Xiaomi’s SU7 Ultra test car points to a more performance-focused model
item.dc:creator: TechNode Feed
item.description: A camouflaged Xiaomi SU7 Ultra test car has appeared in China with a much larger rear wing and other signs of a more aggressive aerodynamic design. The vehicle may be developed as a limited-edition performance model called the SU7 Ultra Extreme. The company has not confirmed the model name, body style, power output or launch […]
item.content:encoded:
A camouflaged Xiaomi SU7 Ultra test car has appeared in China with a much larger rear wing and other signs of a more aggressive aerodynamic design. The vehicle may be developed as a limited-edition performance model called the SU7 Ultra Extreme.

The company has not confirmed the model name, body style, power output or launch schedule. Earlier reports suggested that the vehicle could use a two-door layout and a powertrain exceeding 2,000 horsepower, but those specifications remain unverified. [IT Home, in Chinese]

The update moves the Chinese memory-chip maker further into the exchange’s review process. The change is an IPO milestone rather than a listing approval. ChangXin Memory has not yet completed the offering or received […]
item.content:encoded:
ChangXin Memory’s IPO review status on Shanghai’s STAR Market has changed to “inquiry,” according to information from the Shanghai Stock Exchange. The update moves the Chinese memory-chip maker further into the exchange’s review process.

The change is an IPO milestone rather than a listing approval. ChangXin Memory has not yet completed the offering or received registration approval. [Sina Finance, in Chinese]

item.title: Xiaomi signs first European car dealers ahead of planned overseas launch
item.dc:creator: TechNode Feed
item.description: Xiaomi has signed agreements with its first group of European car dealers at IFA 2026 in Berlin, beginning preparations for the company’s planned overseas sales. The agreements are intended to establish sales channels for Xiaomi vehicles in Europe. Xiaomi has previously said it plans to begin exporting its cars in 2027, starting with developed markets […]
item.content:encoded:
Xiaomi has signed agreements with its first group of European car dealers at IFA 2026 in Berlin, beginning preparations for the company’s planned overseas sales. The agreements are intended to establish sales channels for Xiaomi vehicles in Europe.

Xiaomi has previously said it plans to begin exporting its cars in 2027, starting with developed markets and initially focusing on right-hand-drive countries. The latest agreements mark an early step in that expansion rather than a commercial launch. [IT Home, in Chinese]

item.title: China rolls out a unified three-second mark for special-category micro-dramas
item.dc:creator: TechNode Feed
item.description: China has introduced a unified “Taihua” mark for a special category of micro-dramas under new content-management rules. The mark will appear for three seconds at the beginning of each episode and remain visible in the upper-right corner throughout the episode. The system took effect on September 1, with 11 licensed productions listed as the first […]
item.content:encoded:
China has introduced a unified “Taihua” mark for a special category of micro-dramas under new content-management rules. The mark will appear for three seconds at the beginning of each episode and remain visible in the upper-right corner throughout the episode.

The system took effect on September 1, with 11 licensed productions listed as the first batch. Newly launched productions in the category are expected to adopt the mark by the end of October. [IT Home, in Chinese]

Developer Kacper Skrzypek found related code and renders suggesting a controller with buttons and touch-sensitive grooves that could simulate guitar chords and strumming. The accessory appears to depend on China-focused karaoke app Changba and may […]
item.content:encoded:
Xiaomi may be developing a small flip-style accessory designed to work with the rear screen on its upcoming flagship phones. Developer Kacper Skrzypek found related code and renders suggesting a controller with buttons and touch-sensitive grooves that could simulate guitar chords and strumming.

The accessory appears to depend on China-focused karaoke app Changba and may be designed specifically for Xiaomi phones with rear displays. Xiaomi has not officially confirmed the product or its launch plans. [IT Home, in Chinese]

item.title: ByteDance reportedly lines up a $29.6 billion syndicated loan
item.dc:creator: TechNode Feed
item.description: ByteDance is reportedly preparing to receive a $29.6 billion syndicated loan, after banks showed enough demand for the company to expand the planned facility from $20 billion. The funds would be used for general corporate purposes. The transaction has not yet been formally signed, with banks still confirming their allocations. ByteDance is also reportedly considering […]
item.content:encoded:
ByteDance is reportedly preparing to receive a $29.6 billion syndicated loan, after banks showed enough demand for the company to expand the planned facility from $20 billion. The funds would be used for general corporate purposes.

The transaction has not yet been formally signed, with banks still confirming their allocations. ByteDance is also reportedly considering raising its 2026 capital expenditure to as much as $70 billion, mainly for data centers and other AI infrastructure, although the company has not publicly commented on the financing. [Yicai, in Chinese]

item.title: ChangXin Memory reaches 10% of global DRAM market in Q2
item.dc:creator: TechNode Feed
item.description: ChangXin Memory Technologies, also known as CXMT, held a 10% share of the global DRAM market by revenue in the second quarter, according to the latest data from Counterpoint Research. Its share rose from 4% a year earlier and 8% in the previous quarter, making it the fastest-growing supplier in the market. Samsung Electronics remained […]
item.content:encoded:
ChangXin Memory Technologies, also known as CXMT, held a 10% share of the global DRAM market by revenue in the second quarter, according to the latest data from Counterpoint Research. Its share rose from 4% a year earlier and 8% in the previous quarter, making it the fastest-growing supplier in the market.

Samsung Electronics remained the largest DRAM supplier with a 39% share, followed by SK hynix at 26% and Micron at 25%. The three companies’ combined share fell from 94% to 87% over the same period, while CXMT ranked fourth globally. [IT Home, in Chinese]

item.title: From wild growth to tech-driven growth in China’s AI short drama industry
item.dc:creator: Jessie Wu
item.description: In September, China’s first dedicated departmental regulation for micro-dramas, the Administrative Measures for the Development of Micro-Dramas, officially took effect, bringing AI-generated micro-dramas under a tiered regulatory framework for the first time. The move marks more than just the beginning of a new era of compliance. It signals that China’s AI short drama industry is […]
item.content:encoded:
In September, China’s first dedicated departmental regulation for micro-dramas, the Administrative Measures for the Development of Micro-Dramas, officially took effect, bringing AI-generated micro-dramas under a tiered regulatory framework for the first time.

The move marks more than just the beginning of a new era of compliance. It signals that China’s AI short drama industry is moving beyond its early, anything-goes phase of chasing traffic through sheer production volume and entering a new cycle driven by both technology and content.

The regulation, which came into effect on September 1, places all micro-dramas with individual episodes shorter than 20 minutes under a unified national regulatory framework. It also requires AI-generated micro-dramas to carry prominent AI disclosure labels in every episode.

Streaming platforms are prohibited from using recommendation algorithms designed to encourage excessive consumption or user addiction. By assigning responsibilities across the entire production, review, and distribution process, the rules are pushing the industry away from unchecked growth and toward a healthier ecosystem built around quality and responsible innovation.

Looking back at the explosive growth of the past two years, the first wave of AI short dramas was built largely on the technological dividend of lower costs and higher efficiency. Rapid advances in generative AI have compressed the production costs of short dramas, which could easily run into hundreds of thousands of yuan using traditional methods, to just a few thousand yuan. Projects that once required a crew of more than a dozen people and months of production can now be completed by a single creator using AI tools in just a few weeks.

In the first half of 2026, the industry released 367,000 micro-dramas, with AI-generated productions accounting for more than 74%. More than 1,500 new AI dramas entered the market every day on average, turning the once-theoretical concept of a “one-person production team” into a practical reality for countless small and independent creators.

But the side effects of this rapid, volume-driven growth soon became apparent. Platforms were flooded with interchangeable AI-generated faces and recycled storylines, while the industry-wide rate of recouping production costs remained low.

The resulting bubble of low-quality content threatened to push the entire sector into a vicious cycle where inferior productions crowded out higher-quality work.

The turning point came with the systematic technological upgrades undertaken by leading platforms. Rather than simply opening AI production tools to everyone without restrictions, major players such as ByteDance’s Hongguo Short Drama began building full-stack AI production systems specifically designed for short dramas.

These platforms have fine-tuned large language models specifically for short drama production. They have also used billions of user behavior signals to develop tools that optimize script pacing and reduce low-quality and recycled content at the source.

Platforms are also moving to address some of the technical bottlenecks that have long plagued AI short dramas. Character consistency technology is helping tackle the problem of characters changing appearance across episodes, while multimodal video models are being optimized for the short shots and fast-paced storytelling typical of micro-dramas.

Platforms have also introduced AI content pre-screening systems that can flag issues such as repeated AI-generated faces, potentially infringing materials, and visual defects before a production enters the formal review process.

These efforts point to a broader shift in the industry. AI is no longer being used simply to maximize production volume. Instead, platforms are increasingly applying technology to improve consistency, quality, and compliance throughout the production pipeline. The result is a gradual move away from low-cost mass production toward a more quality-driven model of AI short drama production.

At the same time, a second growth curve for AI short dramas is emerging overseas. From January to July 2026, TikTok short dramas generated more than $110 million in cumulative revenue-sharing payouts, with monthly payouts exceeding $29 million in July alone.

The AI production technologies and highly engaging storytelling formulas refined in China are now being rapidly replicated in global markets, making AI short dramas a new benchmark for China’s digital content exports.

Looking back from this new starting point, AI short dramas were never meant to replace film and television with AI. Their real role is to empower creators by using technology to reshape the economics and relationships of content production.

As low-quality, mass-produced, and recycled content is squeezed out by both regulation and technological advances, the core competitive advantage that will endure is not simply the AI tools themselves, but creators’ ability to accurately capture audience emotions and control narrative pacing.

More value across the AI short drama supply chain is likely to concentrate around leading players with strong IP libraries, foundational AI capabilities, and global distribution networks. China’s experiment with industrializing AI-powered content production has only just entered the stage with the greatest room for imagination.

item.title: Audi opens Shanghai innovation center to develop four AUDI-brand models
item.dc:creator: TechNode Feed
item.description: Audi China has established an innovation technology center in Shanghai with SAIC Group. The center is designed specifically for Audi’s China-focused AUDI brand and will cover vehicle development from product definition and platform engineering to system integration. The two companies plan to use the next-generation Advanced Digital Platform to develop four new AUDI-brand models. The […]
item.content:encoded:
Audi China has established an innovation technology center in Shanghai with SAIC Group. The center is designed specifically for Audi’s China-focused AUDI brand and will cover vehicle development from product definition and platform engineering to system integration.

The two companies plan to use the next-generation Advanced Digital Platform to develop four new AUDI-brand models. The center will focus on electric vehicles, connected-car technologies, AI-powered cockpits and driver-assistance systems for the Chinese market. [IT Home, in Chinese]
